Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights. The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship. Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go. “It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday. The booster was also “slightly low on fuel”, according to SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk. This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX , marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage. It was also only the second time Starship has entered Earth’s orbit. The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission. “Making more believers by the day,” wrote Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman on X, praising the 15th flight. “One step closer to [the moon].” Isaacman is an ally of Musk, who advised Donald Trump to appoint him to lead Nasa. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes. US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations. Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park or its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either. Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation. In a 30-page decision issued on Saturday, Reyes said the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and that the government violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline." "The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote. She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings". Here’s how it works . Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . Justice Anish Kumar Gupta observed that manipulation of age in judicial records amounted to serious misconduct as it constituted “direct interference with the administration of justice”. In an order dated November 2, the court said no lenient view could be taken in cases of such misconduct and dismissed the employee’s writ petition challenging her dismissal from service. The court was hearing a petition filed by Seema Sharma challenging an October 2010 order of the Administrative Judge, which had enhanced the punishment imposed on her by the Muzaffarnagar district judge from stoppage of one increment for two years to dismissal from service. In January 2000, the state government had introduced a scheme for the release of prisoners who had undergone more than three years of imprisonment and were above 60 years of age. Sharma had allegedly manipulated the judicial record of a 1977 sessions trial in which one Juber was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment by a judgment delivered in November 1978. For determining eligibility under the scheme, the prisoner’s age was to be ascertained on the basis of the age mentioned in his statement recorded under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). The original judicial record mentioned Juber’s age as 19 years when his statement was recorded. However, while responding to a questionnaire dated September 13, 2000, Sharma mentioned his age as 38 years, thereby manipulating the record. The discrepancy was subsequently detected, following which an inquiry was conducted. The district judge, Muzaffarnagar, initially imposed the punishment of stoppage of one increment for two years under Rule 4(d) of the Uttar Pradesh Subordinate Court Staff Punishment and Appeal Rules, 1976. However, when Sharma challenged the punishment before the Administrative Judge, the appellate authority considered the charges serious and issued a show-cause notice proposing enhancement of the punishment to dismissal from service. After considering her reply, the Administrative Judge enhanced the punishment to dismissal from service through an order passed in October 2010

Ranchi Chhath Ghats Ready With 1,508 Lights and 88 Generators
clusters.text: Ranchi/Ramgarh: Chhath ghats in Ranchi and Ramgarh are set to host thousands of devotees for the Sandhya Arghya on Sunday.In Ranchi, officials of the Ranchi Municipal Corporation (RMC) inspected the water bodies and arrangements for devotees. Round-the-clock cleaning was carried out across 72 traditional Chhath ghats in the city. That apart, 63 artificial ponds were built across the wards to prevent crowding at the water bodies, officials said.Ranchi municipal commissioner Sushant Gaurav praised the RMC’s civic workforce. “Our teams have been working silently across the city to ensure that the preparations are completed on time. Their efforts are commendable,” he said.Close to 1,400 sanitation workers were deployed for the clean-up. The water bodies have been treated with alum and bleaching powder. Barricades have been put up to keep devotees within safe zones, while over 260 warning signages were installed.Chhath ghats across the city will have 501 temporary changing rooms this year. That apart, 1,508 additional lights have been installed at 83 locations and 88 generators have been arranged to prevent blackouts during rituals. Approach roads have been levelled with stone dust to remove potholes, and open drains along the routes have been covered with slabs to prevent accidents.Local Chhath puja committees have added arrangements at major ponds. At Bada Talab, which sees over 20,000 devotees, Student Federation Chhath Puja Samiti will deploy 76 volunteers for crowd management. Patron Rajiv Ranjan Mishra said, “We are also installing tents, and a Sundarkand Path will be organised at the Surya Mandir in the evening.”At Hataniya Talab, where over 40,000 devotees gather, doctors will be stationed on site. Rajendra Kumar, chairperson of the local Maha Chhath Puja Samiti, said, “A lost-and-found centre will be operational, and the committee is also arranging for milk and fruits to be distributed at the ghat.”Medical teams, first-aid stations and lost-and-found centres have also been arranged at Jail Talab, Button Talab, Karamtoli Talab and Tiril Talab.In Ramgarh, a 45-km stretch of Damodar River, stretching from Bhurkunda to Rajrappa Temple, has been cleaned for the festival. clusters.title: Ranchi Seminary Holds National Seminar on Rebuilding the Church
clusters.text: Ranchi, November 14, 2026: The role of the Church in addressing contemporary social, cultural and ecological challenges came under focus at a national research seminar organised by St. Albert’s College, Ranchi, on November 14. The Annual National Research Seminar 2026–27 brought together theologians, researchers and academicians to discuss the theme, “A Call to Rebuild the Church”, with particular attention to healing, interreligious dialogue, ecological responsibility and the Church’s engagement with indigenous communities. The seminar was inaugurated by lighting a ceremonial lamp in the presence of dignitaries and paper presenters. The Seminary Choir led the opening prayer, while Rector Fr. Ajay Kumar Xalxo welcomed the participants. The first academic session, moderated by Dr. Sushil Kumar Minj, featured three research papers exploring the Church’s response to contemporary challenges. Fr. Valerian Lobo examined the Church’s role as a source of healing, compassion and hope in a divided world. Dr. John Barla OFM Cap presented the theological foundations of Franciscan interreligious dialogue, while Dr. Bhushan Bara explored common perspectives on fraternity, interconnectedness and respect for creation in the spirituality of St. Francis of Assisi and Adivasi traditions. The second session focused on the Church’s mission among indigenous communities in Jharkhand. Prof. Dr. Suman Kumar Ekka highlighted the historical contribution of the Church and its continuing relevance to Adivasi communities. Dr. Raju Felix Crasta, Director of the St. Albert Institute of Philosophy, presented a paper on missionary contributions to the formation of the indigenous Church, with particular reference to Chotanagpur. He stressed the importance of building a Church that respects indigenous culture and identity while encouraging greater participation of local communities. Concluding the seminar, Prof. Dr. Selvaraj highlighted the relevance of the research presentations to the Church’s contemporary mission. Fr. Fabian Kullu, a research scholar, proposed the vote of thanks. The discussions emphasised the need to understand the rebuilding of the Church beyond its institutional structures, focusing instead on a community shaped by healing, dialogue, fraternity and solidarity, and rooted in the cultural and social realities of the people it serves.
